lead: The Sleuth Kit is a set of command-line tools and a code library for analysing disk images and file systems. Autopsy and other forensic programs use it inside.
use_when: You want to see the partition layout of a disk image and list its files, including deleted names.
You want to learn how file systems work by looking at one layer at a time.
You need scripts that run the same steps on many images.

features.title: Image and volume tools
items: mmls shows the partition layout, including unallocated space
img_stat shows details about the image file format
mmstat and mmcat show volume system details and extract a volume

features.title: File system tools
items: fsstat shows file system details such as layout, sizes and labels
fls lists allocated and deleted file names
istat and ils show details of metadata entries
icat extracts a file's data by metadata address, and ifind and ffind link names to metadata

features.title: Data unit and recovery tools
items: blkls can extract the unallocated space of a file system
blkcat and blkstat show the content and details of a data unit
tsk_recover extracts files from an image into a folder, either unallocated files or all files

features.title: Timelines and hashes
items: fls with the -m option writes a body file, and mactime turns it into a file activity timeline
tsk_loaddb loads image metadata into a SQLite database
hfind looks up hashes in databases such as the NIST NSRL
sorter sorts files by type and checks extensions

formats: Split images, by giving the first segment such as .001
requirements: The Sleuth Kit is open source, and the repository includes build notes in INSTALL.txt. Many Linux distributions also offer it as a package. The tools run in a terminal, so you need to be comfortable with command-line basics. Run the tools on a copy of the evidence.

steps.title: Install the tools
steps.text: Install the sleuthkit package from your Linux distribution, or build it from the project's GitHub repository by following INSTALL.txt. Check the tools are available by running a command such as mmls -V, which prints the version.

steps.title: Look at the partition layout
steps.text: Run mmls on your image to list partitions and unallocated space. Note the start sector of the partition you want. If you give the first segment of a split image, such as .001, the rest are included.

steps.title: Show file system details
steps.text: Use fsstat with the -o option and the start sector from mmls to confirm the file system type and layout.

steps.title: List files, including deleted names
steps.text: Run fls with -r to go through all folders and -p to show full paths. The -d option shows only deleted entries. Each line shows a metadata number you can use in the next step.

steps.title: Extract one file
steps.text: Use icat with the metadata number from fls. Send the output to a file in a separate case folder. Add -r to try recovery of a deleted file.

steps.title: Recover many files at once
steps.text: tsk_recover copies unallocated files from the image into an output folder. Add -e to recover all files, both allocated and unallocated. Without -o it handles every volume and saves each to its own folder.

steps.title: Build a timeline
steps.text: Write a body file with fls -m, then convert it with mactime. Use -z to set the time zone of the original system. Add a date range to keep the output short.
steps.cmd:
fls -r -m / -o 2048 image.dd > body.txt
mactime -b body.txt -y > timeline.txt

options.what: Tells fls, icat, fsstat and similar tools where the file system starts in the image, in sectors.
Lists the image formats your build supports. Most tools autodetect the format if you leave -i out.
Lists the supported file system types. Most tools autodetect the type.
Long format with times, size and owner IDs.
Writes comma-delimited output that you can open in a spreadsheet.
Sets the time zone where the data was collected.

cases.title: Checking partitions
cases.why: mmls shows the layout and unallocated gaps, which helps when a partition table looks wrong or hidden.

cases.title: Finding deleted file names
cases.why: fls can list deleted entries, and icat can extract the content where it is still available.

cases.title: Timeline of file activity
cases.why: A body file and mactime give a sorted list of file times for a date range.

cases.title: Bulk recovery
cases.why: tsk_recover copies files from an image to a folder for review in other tools.

cases.title: Hash checking
cases.why: hfind searches hash databases such as the NIST NSRL to find known files.

cases.title: Teaching file system structure
cases.why: Each tool works on one layer, so students can see how names, metadata and data units connect.

strengths: Free and open source, with a library that other tools can use.
Each tool does one job, which makes the steps easy to explain and to script.
Works on image files, so the original disk is not touched.
Manual pages for each tool are published on the project site.
limits: There is no graphical interface. Autopsy provides one on top of these tools.
The tools are low level, so you must know sector offsets and metadata numbers.
It does not parse apps, browsers or the registry on its own.
It reads images but does not create forensic images. Use an imaging tool for that.
The old wiki is no longer maintained, and the project is moving documentation to new sites.
Which image formats work depends on how your copy was built, so check with -i list.
